description: somos un equipo de estudiantes de bachillerato del colegio técnico lorenzo de Salazar (Jesús María ,Santander, Colombia ), guiados por nuestro profesor de informática y robótica educativa. En el colegio trabajamos con Arduino y mictrobit, sensores y prototipos. Participamos en Space App para usar los datos abiertos de la nasa y crear soluciones reales que ayuden a nuestra comunidad.
summary: Orbit is software designed to identify health risk factors for astronauts on future long-duration space missions. It was built with the astronaut's well-being in mind: astronauts enter information about their health directly into the system and, in return, receive clear and precise instructions on what to do. The software approaches the challenge from three angles: using available resources efficiently, supporting astronaut autonomy, and overcoming the difficulty of accessing medical care during expeditions. It matters because it gives the spacecraft crew a medical assistant that is available whenever they need it, one that can guide them step by step through decisions that may determine their survival and well-being. In the future, it will also help people at home and in their communities respond more quickly to a symptom or case that can be analyzed using a large internal or online database.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Orbi is an onboard health assistant that helps astronauts get closer to a possible diagnosis of what they are feeling, through guided questions. Its backbone is a knowledge base built from NASA’s public information on the five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile or closed environments. From this information, we defined standards that link each hazard to its possible effects on the human body.

The astronaut taps the area of an interactive human body where they feel discomfort, and Orbi starts a conversation. Each answer opens a new set of questions, organized as a decision tree, until a probable cause is reached. The result explains what may be happening, what to do right away, and an urgency level: mild, moderate or urgent. Answers that signal danger, such as chest pain or fainting, immediately trigger the urgent level. A vital-signs panel also simulates sensors for each hazard (radiation, cabin CO₂, hours of sleep, bone density, among others), and these readings are used as evidence for the diagnosis.

What benefits does it offer?
It gives astronauts quick, clear guidance when communication with Earth is delayed by several minutes. It reduces uncertainty when a symptom appears, helps recognize urgent situations in time, and keeps a log of every consultation for the flight surgeon. It works offline from a single file and runs on both computers and phones.

What is the intended impact?
We expect Orbi to serve as a first health filter on long missions, such as those to the Moon or Mars, where medical autonomy will be essential. On Earth, it can be adapted for isolated places with little access to doctors, such as rural areas, expeditions or remote bases. It also has educational value: it shows students how NASA science, programming and decision trees come together to solve a real problem.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did we use?

Type of software:
Orbi is a client-side web application, built as a single-page application (SPA) that runs entirely in the web browser. It needs no installation, server or external database, and it works on any device with a modern browser, including computers, tablets and phones, on Windows, Android, iOS or Linux.

By function, Orbi is a rule-based expert system, a type of clinical decision support system (CDSS). Its knowledge base, built from NASA’s information on the five hazards of human spaceflight, is stored as structured data (JavaScript objects in a JSON-like format). A decision-tree inference engine walks through that knowledge base: each answer from the astronaut follows a branch until it reaches a possible cause. The app also includes a sensor telemetry simulator that generates real-time readings for each hazard, which the system uses as additional evidence.

All of it is packaged as a single standalone HTML file, so it works offline. That matters in space, where communication is not always available. It is free, open-source software, hosted on GitHub and published with GitHub Pages.

Software and tools used:

  • Languages: HTML5 for the page structure (header, human body, chat and panels); CSS3 for the design, colors, frosted-glass effect, animations and mobile layout; and plain JavaScript (ES6), with no frameworks or libraries, for the decision tree, the conversation with Orbi, sensor simulation, alerts and the activity log.
  • Graphics: SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) for the holographic human body and trend charts, drawn with code.
  • Typography: Google Fonts (Nunito), with a system-font fallback when offline.
  • AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic), used to help write the code from the team’s ideas and corrections.
  • Image processing: Python with the Pillow library, to compress the background photo and embed it in the file.
  • Testing: Chromium browser automated with Playwright, to check the app on desktop and mobile screen sizes.
  • Version control and hosting: GitHub (repository) and GitHub Pages (live web app).
  • Scientific source: NASA’s information on the hazards of human spaceflight.

How is it creative?
Instead of a cold medical form, Orbi talks to the astronaut in a friendly, informal way and guides them step by step, like a fellow crew member would. It combines three ideas in one tool: an interactive human body to point to the pain, a decision tree that can be viewed in full to understand how the result was reached, and sensors that support or rule out possible causes. In addition, the background is a real sunset from our region, so astronauts can feel close to home while sharing how they feel.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Ease of use: short questions, large buttons and simple language, so astronauts can think quickly even when in pain.
  • Safety: warning signs always lead to the urgent level, and the app makes clear that it offers guidance and the final decision belongs to the flight surgeon.
  • Emotional well-being: a warm tone and a design that is easy on the eyes, keeping in mind the isolation of long missions.
  • Offline operation: everything is in a single file, because communication is not always available in space.
  • Scientific basis: every question and every possible cause is linked to one of NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight.
